posts.body:
Hi!
I believe you should not use the requestAnimationFrame.
Instead, use the update method of the scene if you need something on the game loop.
By default, everything that is added to to the scene as a child, will be already updating together with the update method of the scene.
When you are going to the menu, I believe the requestAnimationFrame are still executing your update function, regardless it is on another scene.
So, try creating a class for your message box, and add it as a child to the scene.

posts.author: caethyril
posts.body:
I would not consider this to be a "simple" plugin.
Like
Game_Message
vs
Window_Message
, or
Game_Temp
vs
Spriteset_Base
&
Sprite_Animation
, you would generally want to create an abstract object, distinct from the PIXI display object, to handle the mechanics separately.
Also, as mentioned by others, your message bubbles would generally be implemented as a new class, probably inheriting from
Window_Base
, and would include an
update
method. The core scenes
update
their children each cycle. So this approach ensures that your additions update in sync with the existing game loop.

FPS is capped to the ticker rate by default: you should at least be looking at frame duration (F2 twice). But afaik a memory leak will typically saturate RAM, with minimal impact (until that point) on other resources. For properly investigating stuff at this level, I'd recommend using the Performance tab of the dev tools window (F8 or F12) rather than relying on tools like the Task Manager.
Also, your test might not even cause a memory leak, depending on how you wrote it. E.g.
PIXI, or the browser/compiler, may skip certain aspects of your test.
If each test replaced the previous one with identical image data, maybe only 1 texture was retained.
The main reason you should call
destroy
is because PIXI's texture batching blocks standard garbage collection. I'm no expert on PIXI...it's possible it implements GC-like checks to compensate for that. Given
destroy
exists, though, I figure it should be used!

posts.author: redeme
posts.body:
I thought the problem was fixed, but I often got a reference error afterwards.
Trigger was quite random, but most of them seemed to be caused by the order of update by fine lag and game speed.
I wanted to expand this structure and implement a lot of things in future, so I kept track what is wrong for a while, In the end, I was able to find the answer by looking back on all of your advice and reviewing my codes.
So the key problem was that the position of Bubble Sprite, an object made of Pixi Sprite, was remotely managed by BubbleManager that the custom class I made.
The update cycle/delete/reference timing of Bubble Sprite was different from that of the Bubble Manager Class, so Bubble Manager kept tried to refer to Bubble when the Pixi Transform of the Bubble was already deleted but not the Bubble itselt yet.
Which resulting in an "error that Bubble exists but cannot refer to the position value".
The solution was that BubbleManager Class only included the Add and Remove of BubbleSprite, Managing queue, and the function that pass the index of each BubbleSprite objects in the queue.
Any reference to the Sprite element, such as the position of the Bubble Sprite, was made to be resolved inside the Bubble Sprite object.
Theoretically by not making remote references, the error can no longer occur anymore, And the error has actually been resolved!
Thank you so much for your help.

Thank you for your advice.
I'm not against your opinion, but it seems that GC in rmmz and js VN is already working brilliantly just by destroying Sprite made of Bitmap.
I wrote a code for test that repeats a series of routines that generate random bitmap, generate Sprite with that bitmap, render it to Scene, and then delete it,
Leaving it for about three or four hours had no effect on FPS and latency, and there was no significant difference in volume of js VN runtime, or Memory size.
(Of course, if you don't destroy the sprite it seems like you keep using the memory)
Until I tested it like this, I definitely thought there would be a stack of bitmap / cache file garbage as you said, but in reality, the built-in memory managing seems to be working hard. It's amazing to me, too.
